clinicalPearls: A very rare defect of red-cell nucleotide metabolism causing chronic non-spherocytic, Coombs-negative haemolytic anaemia
Inherited as an autosomal recessive trait, often with a background of consanguinity
Some affected individuals have shown associated neurological features such as psychomotor impairment, reflecting the enzyme's wider role
The blood film shows non-specific changes without spherocytes, consistent with a metabolic red-cell defect
Haemolysis severity varies widely between reported families, from mild compensated anaemia to transfusion dependence
Diagnosis is by reduced red-cell adenylate kinase activity on assay together with AK1 mutation testing
Management is supportive with folate and transfusion as required, with splenectomy considered only in severe transfusion-dependent disease
reference.pathophysiology: Adenylate kinase catalyses the interconversion of two molecules of ADP into ATP and AMP, helping to buffer the adenine nucleotide pool and maintain the red cell's energy charge. When the enzyme is deficient, the cell's ability to regenerate ATP and preserve nucleotide balance is impaired, which shortens survival and produces a chronic non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia. As the enzyme is also expressed in other tissues, severe deficiency may be accompanied by neurological manifestations in some patients.
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count, reticulocyte count and blood film
Haemolysis screen with bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase and haptoglobin
Direct antiglobulin test to exclude immune haemolysis
Neurological assessment where developmental features are present
Molecular testing of the AK1 gene
redFlags: Severe neonatal jaundice requiring exchange transfusion
Aplastic crisis following parvovirus B19 infection
Progressive neurological impairment in severe cases
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on residual enzyme activity and the presence of neurological involvement; many patients have a mild well-compensated anaemia, while severe cases require ongoing transfusion support.
pitfalls: Assuming a membrane disorder when spherocytes are absent rather than pursuing enzyme assays
Missing associated neurological features that indicate a systemic enzymopathy
Neglecting iron-overload surveillance in transfused patients
Failing to offer genetic counselling given the recessive inheritance
